articles.description: Scientists have discovered a strange form of magnetism in an ordinary-looking metal that has no overall magnetization yet profoundly changes how electrons behave. articles.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick
articles.description: A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck has revealed sophisticated waterproofing techniques involving pine tar and beeswax. Microscopic pollen grains trapped in the ancient coatings are now helping scientists reconstruct where the vessel may have traveled and undergone repairs more than two millennia ago.

articles.title: Cannabis users develop psychosis years earlier, and the gap grows with age
articles.description: A major analysis of 149 studies found that cannabis users develop psychosis an average of 2.5 years earlier than non-users, with the difference growing to more than six years among adults 30 and older. Researchers warn that cannabis-related psychiatric risks may accumulate over time, challenging the belief that using marijuana after adolescence is relatively safe.

articles.title: Scientists discover a new type of depression that common antidepressants struggle to treat
articles.description: Researchers have discovered a new subtype of depression that may affect nearly one in four people with severe, recurrent, or persistent depression. Known as "circadian depression," it is linked to the body's internal clock and is associated with night owl tendencies, excessive sleep, persistent exhaustion, and more severe symptoms. Traditional antidepressants often work less effectively for these individuals, potentially explaining why some people struggle to find relief.

articles.title: Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it
articles.description: Scientists have uncovered surprising evidence that Earth’s next ice age may have already begun, only to be stopped by global warming. By studying ancient plants preserved beneath the Barnes Ice Cap in the Canadian Arctic, researchers discovered that the remnants of a massive ice sheet began expanding again about 2,000 years ago, signaling the possible start of a new glacial period. But by the 1960s, rising temperatures had reversed that growth, causing the ice to shrink instead.
